claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs show normal appearance, self-renewal and growth.
source: ESCs lacking Oct1 show normal appearance, self-renewal and growth but manifest defects upon differentiation.
evidence: Supported by microscopy images (Figure 1A), immunoblot data (Figure 1B), and RT-qPCR data (Figure 1C) showing normal morphology and expression of pluripotency markers.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs fail to form beating cardiomyocytes.
source: ESCs lacking Oct1 show normal appearance, self-renewal and growth but manifest defects upon differentiation. They fail to form beating cardiomyocytes, generate neurons poorly, form small, poorly differentiated teratomas, and cannot generate chimeric mice.
evidence: Supported by cardiomyocyte differentiation assays (Figure 3A) and Videos 1-12 showing lack of beating in Oct1-deficient conditions.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs generate neurons poorly.
source: They fail to form beating cardiomyocytes, generate neurons poorly, form small, poorly differentiated teratomas, and cannot generate chimeric mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 2E-H) showing reduced β-tubulin III-positive neurons and RT-qPCR data (Figure 2I) showing defective expression of neuronal markers.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs form small, poorly differentiated teratomas.
source: They fail to form beating cardiomyocytes, generate neurons poorly, form small, poorly differentiated teratomas, and cannot generate chimeric mice.
evidence: Supported by teratoma mass measurements (Figure 5C) and histological analysis (Figure 5E) showing smaller tumors with immature elements.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs cannot generate chimeric mice.
source: They fail to form beating cardiomyocytes, generate neurons poorly, form small, poorly differentiated teratomas, and cannot generate chimeric mice.
evidence: Supported by blastocyst injection experiments (Figure 5F-G) showing no contribution to adult tissues.

claim: Oct1-deficient cells induce lineage-appropriate developmentally poised genes poorly upon RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, Oct1-deficient cells induce lineage-appropriate developmentally poised genes poorly while lineage-inappropriate genes, including extra-embryonic genes, are aberrantly expressed.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2B) showing defective induction of Hoxa5 and Hoxc6, and RNAseq data (Figure 6E) showing poor induction of multiple developmental genes.

claim: Oct1-deficient cells aberrantly express lineage-inappropriate genes, including extra-embryonic genes, upon RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, Oct1-deficient cells induce lineage-appropriate developmentally poised genes poorly while lineage-inappropriate genes, including extra-embryonic genes, are aberrantly expressed.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2B) showing ectopic expression of Cdx2 and Sox17, and RNAseq data (Figure 6F) showing aberrant expression of placental genes like Prl8a6.

claim: Oct1 co-occupies a specific set of targets with Oct4 in ESCs.
source: In ESCs, Oct1 co-occupies a specific set of targets with Oct4, but does not occupy differentially expressed developmental targets.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data (Figure 7A) showing 356 common targets between Oct1 and Oct4.

claim: Oct1 does not occupy differentially expressed developmental targets in ESCs.
source: In ESCs, Oct1 co-occupies a specific set of targets with Oct4, but does not occupy differentially expressed developmental targets.
evidence: Supported by intersection of ChIPseq and RNAseq data (Figure 7A) showing little overlap between Oct1-bound genes and differentially expressed genes.

claim: Oct1 occupies developmental targets as cells differentiate and Oct4 declines.
source: Instead, Oct1 occupies these targets as cells differentiate and Oct4 declines.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data (Figure 8F) showing Oct1 binding to Hoxc5, Myf5, Rest, and Pou5f1 during differentiation.

claim: Oct4 is an indispensable component of the regulatory circuitry underlying ESC pluripotency.
source: The POU transcription factor Oct4/Pou5f1 is an indispensable component of the regulatory circuitry underlying these properties (Morey et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morey et al., 2015.

claim: Oct4 is expressed in the ICM and in ESCs where its loss accompanies differentiation.
source: It is expressed in the ICM and in ESCs where its loss accompanies differentiation (Nichols et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nichols et al., 1998.

claim: Oct4 is widely used to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from somatic cells.
source: Oct4 is also widely used to generate induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from somatic cells (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: Oct4 sustains pluripotency by activating 'core' targets such as Pou5f1 and Nanog.
source: Together with other factors, Oct4 sustains pluripotency by activating 'core' targets such as Pou5f1 (encoding Oct4 itself) and Nanog (Boyer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boyer et al., 2005.

claim: Oct4 maintains 'poised' targets, including developmentally critical transcription regulators, in a silent but readily inducible state.
source: It also maintains 'poised' targets, including developmentally critical transcription regulators, in a silent but readily inducible state (Bernstein et al., 2006; Meissner et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2006 and Meissner et al., 2008.

claim: Poised genes frequently encode developmentally important transcription factors and are marked with a bivalent chromatin signature defined by the simultaneous presence of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3.
source: These genes frequently encode developmentally important transcription factors and are marked with a bivalent chromatin signature defined by the simultaneous presence of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 (Azuara et al., 2006; Bernstein et al., 2006; Ku et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Azuara et al., 2006; Bernstein et al., 2006; Ku et al., 2008; Pan et al., 2007.

claim: Oct1 is a widely expressed protein related to Oct4.
source: Oct1/Pou2f1 is a widely expressed protein related to Oct4.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Oct1.

claim: Oct1 and Oct4 have similar DNA-binding specificity.
source: The two proteins have similar DNA-binding specificity (Tantin, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tantin, 2013.

claim: In somatic cells, Oct1 regulates stem cell and immune memory phenotypes.
source: In somatic cells, it regulates stem cell and immune memory phenotypes (Maddox et al., 2012; Shakya et al., 2015b) and is associated with cytotoxic stress resistance, glycolytic metabolism and malignant transformation (Bellance et al., 2012; Shakya et al., 2009; Tantin et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maddox et al., 2012 and Shakya et al., 2015b.

claim: Oct1 is associated with cytotoxic stress resistance, glycolytic metabolism and malignant transformation.
source: In somatic cells, it regulates stem cell and immune memory phenotypes (Maddox et al., 2012; Shakya et al., 2015b) and is associated with cytotoxic stress resistance, glycolytic metabolism and malignant transformation (Bellance et al., 2012; Shakya et al., 2009; Tantin et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bellance et al., 2012; Shakya et al., 2009; Tantin et al., 2005.

claim: Oct1 amplification and/or overexpression correlates with tumor aggressiveness in esophageal, gastric, prostate, lung, cervical, and colorectal cancer.
source: Oct1 amplification and/or overexpression correlates with tumor aggressiveness in esophageal, gastric, prostate, lung, cervical, and colorectal cancer (Vázquez-Arreguín and Tantin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vázquez-Arreguín and Tantin, 2016.

claim: Oct1 is co-expressed with Oct4 in ESCs.
source: It is also co-expressed with Oct4 in ESCs (Okamoto et al., 1990; Rosner et al., 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Okamoto et al., 1990 and Rosner et al., 1990.

claim: Oct1-deficient mice undergo implantation but show defects following gastrulation, most prominently in extra-embryonic tissues.
source: Oct1-deficient mice undergo implantation but show defects following gastrulation, most prominently in extra-embryonic tissues, where trophoblast stem cell development is arrested and expression of the direct Oct1 target Cdx2 is defective (Sebastiano et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebastiano et al., 2010.

claim: In Oct1-deficient mice, trophoblast stem cell development is arrested and expression of the direct Oct1 target Cdx2 is defective.
source: Oct1-deficient mice undergo implantation but show defects following gastrulation, most prominently in extra-embryonic tissues, where trophoblast stem cell development is arrested and expression of the direct Oct1 target Cdx2 is defective (Sebastiano et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebastiano et al., 2010.

claim: Tetraploid complementation bypasses the developmental restriction in Oct1-deficient mice, allowing embryos to survive to E8.5–9.5 where they die from an embryo-intrinsic block.
source: Tetraploid complementation bypasses this developmental restriction, allowing embryos to survive to E8.5–9.5 where they die from an embryo-intrinsic block. These embryos are runted, developmentally arrested, and lack beating hearts. (Sebastiano et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebastiano et al., 2010.

claim: Oct1-deficient embryos generated by tetraploid complementation are runted, developmentally arrested, and lack beating hearts.
source: These embryos are runted, developmentally arrested, and lack beating hearts. (Sebastiano et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebastiano et al., 2010.

claim: A slightly less severe germline Oct1 allele dies in mid-gestation and manifests runting, anemia, hemorrhaging, and other defects with variable penetrance.
source: A slightly less severe germline allele dies in mid-gestation and manifests runting, anemia, hemorrhaging, and other defects with variable penetrance (Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs have normal karyotypes.
source: All had normal karyotypes (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on karyotype analysis.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs proliferate at normal rates.
source: Oct1-deficient ESCs proliferate at normal rates (not shown), are morphologically normal (Figure 1A) and can be propagated for a month in culture with no loss of ESC morphology (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on proliferation assays.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs are morphologically normal.
source: Oct1-deficient ESCs proliferate at normal rates (not shown), are morphologically normal (Figure 1A) and can be propagated for a month in culture with no loss of ESC morphology (not shown).
evidence: Supported by phase microscopy images in Figure 1A.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs can be propagated for a month in culture with no loss of ESC morphology.
source: Oct1-deficient ESCs proliferate at normal rates (not shown), are morphologically normal (Figure 1A) and can be propagated for a month in culture with no loss of ESC morphology (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on long-term culture observations.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs express normal levels of Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog protein.
source: They express normal levels of Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog protein but no Oct1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs express no Oct1 protein.
source: They express normal levels of Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog protein but no Oct1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 1B.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs express Pou5f1, Sox2, Nanog, and Dppa4 mRNAs at normal levels.
source: In addition, cells express the pluripotency-associated Pou5f1 (Oct4), Sox2, Nanog, and Dppa4 mRNAs at normal levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1C.

claim: Ahcy expression is unaltered in Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: Ahcy, a stress-inducible Oct1 target in which the function of Oct1 is to prevent stress-associated repression (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011), was also unaltered.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1C and citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs can aggregate into EBs at day 4 with morphology similar to WT.
source: Oct1-deficient ESCs were able to aggregate into EBs at d four with morphology similar to WT (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by phase microscopy images in Figure 1D.

claim: During EB formation, Pou5f1 and Sox2 are down-modulated with similar kinetics in Oct1-deficient and WT cells.
source: During EB formation, Pou5f1 and Sox2 were down-modulated with similar kinetics in Oct1-deficient and WT cells, while Pou2f1 (Oct1) remained undetectable (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 1E.

claim: Sox17, T, and Fgf5 expression in Oct1-deficient EBs is grossly similar to WT at some timepoints.
source: Sox17 (endoderm), Brachyury (T, definitive mesoderm), and Fgf5 (definitive ectoderm) expression in Oct1-deficient EBs was grossly similar to WT at some (days 4, 9, or 14) timepoints (Figure 1F), consistent with findings that Oct1 is dispensable for gastrulation (Sebastiano et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1F and citations to Sebastiano et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2004.

claim: Oct1-deficient EBs show consistent defects in Sox17 expression at day 14 and in T and Fgf5 expression at day 4.
source: However, there were consistent defects in expression in the Oct1-deficient condition at day 14 for Sox17 and day 4 for T and Fgf5.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1F.

claim: Sox17, T and Fgf5 are known Oct4 targets.
source: Sox17, T and Fgf5 are known Oct4 targets (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Oct1-deficient EBs are somewhat smaller in appearance by day 5.
source: By day 5, Oct1-deficient EBs were somewhat smaller in appearance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Hoxa5, Hoxc6, and Gata2 show defective induction in Oct1-deficient EBs relative to WT controls.
source: Each of these genes showed a similar pattern of defective induction in Oct1-deficient EBs relative to WT controls (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 1G.

claim: Hoxa5, Hoxc6, and Gata2 are known silent but developmentally inducible Oct4 target genes.
source: We therefore looked for further evidence of defects in induction kinetics in three other known silent but developmentally inducible Oct4 target genes: Hoxa5, Hoxc6, and Gata2 (Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2008.

claim: RA treatment of ESCs ultimately results in a largely neuronal phenotype.
source: RA treatment of ESCs ultimately results in a largely neuronal phenotype, but waves of gene expression, differentiation, proliferation, and cell death take place during the course of RA treatment (Walker et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2007.

claim: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, ESCs ±Oct1 lose their clustered, spherical, refractile morphology with similar kinetics.
source: Upon differentiation, ESCs ±Oct1 lose their clustered, spherical, refractile morphology with similar kinetics (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on microscopic observations.

claim: Pou5f1 and Sox2 are lost with similar kinetics ±Oct1 upon RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Pou5f1 and Sox2 were also lost with similar kinetics ±Oct1, while Pou2f1 was not detectable in KO cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2A.

claim: Hoxa5, Hoxc6, Cdx2, and Sox17 encode developmentally important transcription factors and are known Oct4 targets.
source: These genes encode developmentally important transcription factors and are known Oct4 targets (Chen et al., 2008), but are silent in ESCs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2008.

claim: Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 are lineage-appropriate (ectoderm) genes.
source: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, lineage-appropriate (ectoderm) genes such as Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 (Jiang et al., 2011) normally 'resolve' their bivalent state by losing H3K27me3 and becoming induced, while lineage-inappropriate (e.g. endoderm) genes such as Cdx2 and Sox17 normally resolve by losing H3K4me3, gaining DNA methylation, and becoming stably silenced.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2011.

claim: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, lineage-appropriate genes normally resolve their bivalent state by losing H3K27me3 and becoming induced.
source: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, lineage-appropriate (ectoderm) genes such as Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 (Jiang et al., 2011) normally 'resolve' their bivalent state by losing H3K27me3 and becoming induced, while lineage-inappropriate (e.g. endoderm) genes such as Cdx2 and Sox17 normally resolve by losing H3K4me3, gaining DNA methylation, and becoming stably silenced.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bivalent chromatin resolution during differentiation.

claim: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, lineage-inappropriate genes normally resolve by losing H3K4me3, gaining DNA methylation, and becoming stably silenced.
source: Upon RA-mediated differentiation, lineage-appropriate (ectoderm) genes such as Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 (Jiang et al., 2011) normally 'resolve' their bivalent state by losing H3K27me3 and becoming induced, while lineage-inappropriate (e.g. endoderm) genes such as Cdx2 and Sox17 normally resolve by losing H3K4me3, gaining DNA methylation, and becoming stably silenced.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bivalent chromatin resolution during differentiation.

claim: Induction of Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 is robust following RA-mediated differentiation of WT cells, but defective in the Oct1 KO condition.
source: Induction of Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 was robust following RA-mediated differentiation of WT cells, but defective in the Oct1 KO condition (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Cdx2 is ectopically activated upon RA-mediated differentiation of Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: In contrast, Cdx2 was ectopically activated upon RA-mediated differentiation of Oct1-deficient ESCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Sox17 is not normally induced upon RA-mediated differentiation, but shows ectopic expression in the absence of Oct1.
source: Similarly, the definitive endoderm-specific gene Sox17 is not normally induced upon RA-mediated differentiation, but showed ectopic expression in the absence of Oct1 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2B.

claim: Restoration of Oct1 expression during differentiation can correct some of the gene expression defects associated with Oct1 deficiency.
source: These results indicate that restoration of Oct1 expression at these times and conditions can correct at least some of the gene expression defects associated with Oct1 deficiency.
evidence: Supported by lentiviral complementation experiment (Figure 2D) showing increased Hoxa5 expression upon Oct1 restoration.

claim: RA-mediated differentiation yields neuronal precursor cells but not neurons.
source: RA-mediated differentiation yields neuronal precursor cells but not neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RA differentiation protocols.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs show fewer β-tubulin III-positive cells early in neuronal differentiation.
source: Staining of 2-day-old EBs for β-tubulin III prior to laminin/poly-L-lysine dish attachment – early in the differentiation protocol - revealed fewer β-tubulin III-positive cells in the Oct1 deficient condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Upon complete neuronal differentiation, WT ESCs form neurons robustly while few β-tubulin III-expressing neurons are formed from Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: Upon complete differentiation (8 d EBs, 8 days in neuralizing monolayer culture), WT ESCs formed neurons robustly (Figure 2E, asterisk) while few β-tubulin III-expressing neurons were formed from Oct1-deficient ESCs.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Oct1-deficient cells that induce β-tubulin III tend to do so at lower levels and are abnormal.
source: Oct1-deficient cells that did induce β-tubulin III tended to do so at lower levels, and the few cells that did express β-tubulin III robustly were nevertheless abnormal (Figure 2E–F, arrow).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Longer culture does not overcome the neuronal differentiation defect in Oct1-deficient cells.
source: To test if Oct1 loss induced a kinetic delay that could be overcome by longer culture, cells were incubated for 8 or 16 additional days (16 or 24 days in neuralizing medium, 24 or 32 days total differentiation). In neither case were neurons formed (Figure 2G–H and data not shown).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence images and quantification in Figure 2G-H.

claim: Tubb3, Nes and Map2 show defective expression in Oct1-deficient cells during neuronal differentiation.
source: Each of these genes showed defective expression in the absence of Oct1 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 2I.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs fail to form beating cardiomyocytes.
source: Oct1-deficient ESCs failed to form beating cardiomyocytes, unlike WT (Figure 3A and Videos 1–12).
evidence: Supported by cardiomyocyte differentiation assay in Figure 3A and Videos 1-12.

claim: Mlc2v expression is defective in Oct1-deficient cardiomyocyte differentiation, equivalent to non-beating WT cardiomyocyte colonies.
source: We observed Mlc2v expression defects in the Oct1-deficient condition equivalent to non-beating cardiomyocyte colonies from WT ESCs.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3B.

claim: Mlc2a and Mef2c expression in Oct1-deficient cardiomyocyte differentiation is weaker than non-beating WT cardiomyocyte colonies.
source: Mlc2a and Mef2c expression was even weaker than non-beating WT cardiomyocyte colonies (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3B.

claim: Hand1 shows no expression defects in Oct1-deficient cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: In contrast, Hand1 showed no expression defects (Figure 3B), indicating that Oct1 deficiency does not globally down-regulate genes associated with cardiomyocyte differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 3B.

claim: Oct1 deficiency does not globally down-regulate genes associated with cardiomyocyte differentiation.
source: In contrast, Hand1 showed no expression defects (Figure 3B), indicating that Oct1 deficiency does not globally down-regulate genes associated with cardiomyocyte differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the selective nature of gene expression defects in cardiomyocyte differentiation.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines display normal colony morphology.
source: As with Oct1 germline-deficient ESCs, derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines displayed normal colony morphology (Figure 4C), proliferated normally (not shown) yet expressed no Oct1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 4C.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines proliferate normally.
source: As with Oct1 germline-deficient ESCs, derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines displayed normal colony morphology (Figure 4C), proliferated normally (not shown) yet expressed no Oct1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Stated in the text based on proliferation assays.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines express no Oct1.
source: As with Oct1 germline-deficient ESCs, derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines displayed normal colony morphology (Figure 4C), proliferated normally (not shown) yet expressed no Oct1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines show normal karyotype profiles.
source: The derived cells showed normal karyotype profiles and could be propagated for >1 month without loss of an undifferentiated phenotype (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on karyotype analysis.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESC lines can be propagated for >1 month without loss of an undifferentiated phenotype.
source: The derived cells showed normal karyotype profiles and could be propagated for >1 month without loss of an undifferentiated phenotype (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on long-term culture observations.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells express Oct4, Sox2 and Nanog at normal levels.
source: Similar to germline Oct1 deficient ESCs, derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells also expressed Oct4, Sox2 and Nanog at normal levels (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data in Figure 4D.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs lose Oct4 and Sox2 expression with kinetics identical to the parent line upon RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Similar to results using Oct1 germline-deficient ESCs, the derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs lost Oct4 and Sox2 expression with kinetics identical to the parent line (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4E.

claim: Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells show an increase in columnar/epithelial appearance at approximately day 12 of RA differentiation.
source: Microscopic imaging of the differentiating cells revealed that they were morphologically similar until approximately d 12, at which point Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells showed an increase in columnar/epithelial appearance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 show reduced expression in derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells upon RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Also as before, the induction of silent, developmentally poised genes was defective: Hoxa5 and Hoxc6 both showed reduced expression in timecourse assays (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: Derived Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells show ectopic Cdx2 expression upon RA treatment.
source: The cells also showed ectopic Cdx2 expression upon RA treatment (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4F.

claim: Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs do not generate true neurons efficiently.
source: As with germline-deficient ESCs, Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs did not generate true neurons efficiently (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Nearly all cells that induce β-tubulin III and/or generate neuron morphology lack YFP expression when Oct1 is conditionally deleted during differentiation.
source: 40–50% of the treated cells induced YFP. Nearly all cells that induced β-tubulin III and/or generated neuron morphology lacked YFP expression (Figure 4I and Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4I-J.

claim: Few differences in metabolic profile are noted in ESCs lacking Oct1.
source: Few differences were noted, with only phosphoethanolamine (also known as phosphorylethanolamine, p=0.047) and inositol (p=0.037) showing significant changes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lack of metabolic differences in Oct1-deficient ESCs may be due to redundant functions of co-expressed Oct4 and Oct6.
source: The lack of difference may be due to redundant functions of co-expressed Oct4 and Oct6, or co-selection for metabolic stability when selecting and propagating ESCs.
evidence: This is speculation about why metabolic differences are not observed.

claim: Parent ESCs generate mature teratomas that include glial tissue, glandular epithelial and squamous elements.
source: Histological analysis confirmed that parent cells generated mature teratomas that included, e.g., glial tissue, and glandular epithelial and squamous elements (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 5E.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs generate areas of focally immature cells, consistent with reduced differentiation.
source: In contrast, Oct1 deficient ESCs generated areas of focally immature cells, consistent with reduced differentiation.
evidence: Supported by histological analysis in Figure 5E.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESC-derived teratomas are occasionally comprised virtually entirely of primitive malignant cells resembling a germ cell tumor.
source: Occasionally tumors were comprised virtually entirely of primitive malignant cells resembling a germ cell tumor (Figure 5E, lower right).
evidence: Supported by histological images in Figure 5E.

claim: Parent ESCs show high contribution to chimeric mice when injected into blastocysts.
source: We injected parent and Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs into albino C57BL/6 blastocysts, resulting in high contribution in the case of the parent line (Figure 5F, left), but no contribution in the case of the derived lines (right).
evidence: Supported by chimera images in Figure 5F.

claim: Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs show no contribution to chimeric mice when injected into blastocysts.
source: We injected parent and Pou2f1Δ/Δ ESCs into albino C57BL/6 blastocysts, resulting in high contribution in the case of the parent line (Figure 5F, left), but no contribution in the case of the derived lines (right).
evidence: Supported by chimera images and quantification in Figure 5F-G.

claim: 55% of animals injected with parent ESCs showed some detectable chimerism.
source: 18/33 animals injected with parent ESCs showed some detectable chimerism (55%), while 1/36 animals injected with conditional knockout ESCs showed transient trace chimerism in the eye (0.03%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of chimera experiments in Figure 5G.

claim: Only 1/36 animals injected with conditional knockout ESCs showed transient trace chimerism in the eye.
source: 18/33 animals injected with parent ESCs showed some detectable chimerism (55%), while 1/36 animals injected with conditional knockout ESCs showed transient trace chimerism in the eye (0.03%).
evidence: Supported by quantification of chimera experiments in Figure 5G.

claim: Between 18.1 and 24.9 million sequence reads were generated for each RNAseq sample.
source: Between 18.1 and 24.9 million sequence reads were generated for each sample, 73% to 82% of which aligned uniquely to the mouse Mm10 reference genome.
evidence: This is a description of the RNAseq data quality.

claim: 73% to 82% of RNAseq reads aligned uniquely to the mouse Mm10 reference genome.
source: Between 18.1 and 24.9 million sequence reads were generated for each sample, 73% to 82% of which aligned uniquely to the mouse Mm10 reference genome.
evidence: This is a description of the RNAseq data quality.

claim: 99.6% of RNAseq reads within coding regions aligned to the correct strand.
source: 99.6% of the reads within coding regions aligned to the correct strand.
evidence: This is a description of the RNAseq data quality.

claim: The effect of RA treatment and differentiation on gene expression is far stronger than the effect of Oct1 deletion.
source: These results indicated that the effect of RA treatment and differentiation on gene expression was far stronger than the effect of Oct1 deletion.
evidence: Inferred from unsupervised hierarchical clustering showing samples cluster by differentiation state rather than genotype.

claim: 253 genes show differential expression (>2.5 fold, p<0.01) in undifferentiated Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: Plotting gene expression levels in the parent vs Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells (Figure 6A) showed relatively few gene expression changes in the undifferentiated condition (>2.5 fold, p<0.01, 253 total genes).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Genes differentially expressed in undifferentiated Oct1-deficient ESCs never change by >7 fold.
source: These genes never changed by >7 fold (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 1123 genes show differential expression in differentiated Oct1-deficient cells.
source: In contrast, 1123 genes change expression in differentiated Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells, some of which varied by >200 fold.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Some genes in differentiated Oct1-deficient cells vary by >200 fold.
source: In contrast, 1123 genes change expression in differentiated Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells, some of which varied by >200 fold.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis in Figure 6A.

claim: Only 23 genes are differentially expressed at both undifferentiated and differentiated timepoints in Oct1-deficient cells.
source: Comparing genes differentially expressed at the two timepoints revealed little overlap (23 genes, Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of Tbp is unaltered in Oct1-deficient cells.
source: Analysis of the genomic alignments revealed that expression of control genes such as Tbp was unaltered, while pluripotency genes such as Nanog were silenced equivalently (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6D.

claim: Pluripotency genes such as Nanog are silenced equivalently in Oct1-deficient and WT cells upon differentiation.
source: Analysis of the genomic alignments revealed that expression of control genes such as Tbp was unaltered, while pluripotency genes such as Nanog were silenced equivalently (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6D.

claim: Pou5f1, Klf4, Dnmt3l, and Dppa4 behave similarly to Nanog upon differentiation.
source: Other pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1, Klf4, Dnmt3l, and Dppa4 behaved similarly to Nanog (not shown).
evidence: Stated in the text based on RNAseq analysis.

claim: Pou2f3 shows low but detectable mRNA expression in WT ESCs and is repressed upon differentiation to nearly undetectable levels.
source: Pou2f3 shows low but detectable mRNA expression in WT ESCs, and is repressed upon differentiation to nearly undetectable levels.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and RT-qPCR in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pou2f3 is slightly elevated in Oct1-deficient ESCs but decreases to an even greater extent upon differentiation.
source: It is slightly elevated in Oct1-deficient ESCs but decreases to an even greater extent upon differentiation.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and RT-qPCR in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pou2f3 is unlikely to provide a compensatory function upon differentiation.
source: It is therefore unlikely that this protein provides a compensatory function upon differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the low expression and further decrease upon differentiation.

claim: Approximately 300 genes are induced poorly in RA treated Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells relative to normal controls.
source: Approximately 300 genes were induced poorly in RA treated Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells relative to normal controls.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis.

claim: Many genes induced poorly in RA treated Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells encode regulators of neuronal specification and differentiation.
source: Many of these encode regulators of neuronal specification and differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the identity of the genes showing defective induction.

claim: Ahcy shows weakened expression in the absence of Oct1 specifically in the differentiated condition.
source: In addition, Ahcy, a stress-responsive Oct1 target (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011) showed weakened expression in the absence of Oct1 specifically in the differentiated condition (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6E and citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: An even larger cohort of ~800 genes is aberrantly expressed upon differentiation of Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells.
source: An even larger cohort of ~800 genes was aberrantly expressed upon differentiation of Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq analysis.

claim: Genes aberrantly expressed upon differentiation of Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells are strongly associated with alternative developmental fates.
source: These genes are strongly associated with alternative developmental fates (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq genome tracks in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Differentiating Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells show inappropriate expression of genes associated with trophoblast and placental development.
source: Unexpectedly, differentiating Pou2f1Δ/Δ cells also resulted in inappropriate expression of genes associated with trophoblast and placental development, the specification of which is normally restricted to trophectoderm cells rather than the inner cell mass (from which ESCs are derived).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing expression of placental genes like Prl8a6, Prl3b1, etc.

claim: Oct1 deficiency results in defective lineage specification upon differentiation.
source: These results indicate that Oct1 deficiency results in defective lineage specification upon differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the combined gene expression defects observed in RNAseq.

claim: After filtering, 27.3 million Oct1 and 23.7 million Oct4 alignable ChIPseq reads were generated.
source: After filtering, 27.3 (Oct1), and 23.7 (Oct4) million alignable reads were generated, corresponding to 692 (Oct1), and 8673 (Oct4) peaks.
evidence: This is a description of the ChIPseq data quality.

claim: 692 Oct1 peaks and 8673 Oct4 peaks were identified by ChIPseq.
source: After filtering, 27.3 (Oct1), and 23.7 (Oct4) million alignable reads were generated, corresponding to 692 (Oct1), and 8673 (Oct4) peaks.
evidence: This is a description of the ChIPseq results.

claim: Allocating ChIPseq peaks to nearest genes revealed 209 unique Oct1 target genes, 356 common targets, and 5563 unique Oct4 targets.
source: Allocating the peaks to nearest genes revealed 209 unique Oct1 target genes, 356 common targets, and 5563 unique Oct4 targets (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram in Figure 7A.

claim: The smaller size of the Oct1 target pool relative to Oct4 may be attributable to >10 fold lower Oct1 levels in ESCs.
source: The smaller size of the Oct1 target pool relative to Oct4 may be attributable to >10 fold lower Oct1 levels in ESCs as observed by RT-qPCR (Figure 1C, Figure 1E, Figure 2A) and RNAseq (not shown).
evidence: This is speculation about why Oct1 has fewer targets than Oct4.

claim: Oct1 may require a more open chromatin context, and/or the presence of specific co-bound factors, to access DNA.
source: Oct1 may also require a more open chromatin context, and/or the presence of specific co-bound factors, to access DNA.
evidence: This is speculation about Oct1 binding requirements.

claim: Il2 and Ifng are known Oct1 targets in differentiated T cells but were not identified as targets in ESCs.
source: For example Il2 and Ifng are known Oct1 targets in differentiated T cells (Shakya et al., 2015b, 2011) but were not identified as targets in this analysis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Shakya et al., 2015b and 2011.

claim: Regions associated exclusively with Oct4 are significantly enriched for Oct-Sox compound elements.
source: Motif analysis of unique and co-bound peaks revealed significant differences in recognized DNA elements. Regions associated exclusively with Oct4 were significantly enriched for Oct-Sox compound elements that likely also associate with Sox2 in ESCs (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: Target regions preferentially associated with Oct1 are enriched for the simple octamer element ATTTGCAT.
source: In contrast, target regions preferentially associated with Oct1 were enriched for the simple octamer element ATTTGCAT (shown by the software as an Oct4 motif in Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis in Figure 7B.

claim: Co-occupied peaks strongly associate with a motif termed a MORE that is known to bind two Oct protein molecules.
source: Interestingly, co-occupied peaks strongly associate with a motif termed a MORE that is known to bind two Oct protein molecules (Reményi et al., 2001; Tomilin et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis in Figure 7B and citations to Reményi et al., 2001 and Tomilin et al., 2000.

claim: In differentiated cells lacking Oct4, oxidative stress induces homodimeric Oct1 binding to MORE-containing genes such as Polr2a, Ahcy, Ell, and Rras2.
source: In differentiated cells lacking Oct4, oxidative stress induces homodimeric Oct1 binding to MORE-containing genes such as Polr2a, Ahcy, Ell, and Rras2.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work (Kang et al., 2009).

claim: Oxidative stress-induced Oct1 binding occurs via phosphorylation of a conserved serine residue in the DNA-binding domain.
source: Oxidative stress-induced binding occurs via phosphorylation of a conserved serine residue in the DNA-binding domain (Kang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 2009.

claim: Polr2a, Ahcy, Ell, and Rras2 are constitutively co-bound by Oct1 and Oct4 in ESCs.
source: These genes were constitutively co-bound by Oct1 and Oct4 in ESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq genome tracks in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 34 Oct1-bound or Oct1/Oct4 co-bound targets show differential expression following RA-mediated differentiation.
source: Intersecting the ChIPseq and RNAseq data revealed little overlap. Only 34 Oct1-bound or Oct1/Oct4 co-bound targets showed differential expression following RA-mediated differentiation (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram in Figure 7A.

claim: 193 Oct1-bound and 325 Oct1/Oct4-co-bound genes do not show expression differences at day 14 of differentiation.
source: 193 Oct1-bound and 325 Oct1/Oct4-co-bound genes did not show expression differences at d 14.
evidence: Supported by intersection of ChIPseq and RNAseq data.

claim: 1066 genes with altered expression in differentiated Oct1-deficient cells show Oct4 but not Oct1 enrichment in ESCs.
source: Instead, 1066 genes with altered expression in differentiated Oct1-deficient cells showed Oct4 but not Oct1 enrichment.
evidence: Supported by intersection of ChIPseq and RNAseq data in Figure 7A.

claim: Identified Oct1 targets are not differentially expressed upon differentiation.
source: These findings indicate that (1) identified Oct1 targets were not differentially expressed upon differentiation, and (2) developmental genes shown to be differentially expressed in RA treated Oct1-deficient cells were not Oct1 targets in ESCs.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of overlap between ChIPseq and RNAseq data.

claim: Developmental genes differentially expressed in RA treated Oct1-deficient cells are not Oct1 targets in ESCs.
source: These findings indicate that (1) identified Oct1 targets were not differentially expressed upon differentiation, and (2) developmental genes shown to be differentially expressed in RA treated Oct1-deficient cells were not Oct1 targets in ESCs.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of overlap between ChIPseq and RNAseq data.

claim: Oct1 functions at co-bound targets in ESCs to buffer them against oxidative stress.
source: The above findings could be reconciled by postulating that (1) Oct functions at co-bound targets in ESCs to buffer them against oxidative stress as described previously in fibroblasts (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011), and (2) developmental genes that are differentially expressed in Oct1-deficient cells but exclusively bound by Oct4 in ESCs become Oct1 targets during the differentiation process as Oct4 is lost.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to reconcile the ChIPseq and RNAseq findings, supported by citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Developmental genes that are differentially expressed in Oct1-deficient cells but exclusively bound by Oct4 in ESCs become Oct1 targets during the differentiation process as Oct4 is lost.
source: The above findings could be reconciled by postulating that (1) Oct functions at co-bound targets in ESCs to buffer them against oxidative stress as described previously in fibroblasts (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011), and (2) developmental genes that are differentially expressed in Oct1-deficient cells but exclusively bound by Oct4 in ESCs become Oct1 targets during the differentiation process as Oct4 is lost.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to reconcile the ChIPseq and RNAseq findings.

claim: Treatment of ESCs with 2 mM H2O2 results in a rapid loss of Ahcy and Polr2a mRNA specifically in Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: Treatment of cells with 2 mM H2O2 resulted in a rapid loss of Ahcy and Polr2a mRNA specifically in Oct1-deficient ESCs (Figure 8B), exactly as observed in fibroblasts (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 8B and citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Oct1-deficient ESCs are hypersensitive to H2O2.
source: As expected, these cells were hypersensitive to H2O2 (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 8C.

claim: As in other cell types, Oct1 functions in ESCs to buffer genes from oxidative stress-associated inhibition.
source: These results suggest that as in other cell types, Oct1 functions in ESCs to buffer these genes from oxidative stress-associated inhibition.
evidence: Inferred from the H2O2 treatment experiments.

claim: Oct1 binding to Hoxc5 is transiently observed at 6 days of differentiation.
source: Oct1 ChIP-qPCR revealed no binding in ESCs, as expected based on the ChIPseq (Figure 8F), however robust binding was transiently observed at 6 d.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Oct1 binding to Hoxc5 is undetectable by 14 days of differentiation.
source: By 14 d of differentiation Oct1 binding was again undetectable.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Oct1 inducibly occupies the Myf5/Myf6 region at 2 days of differentiation as Oct4 binding is lost.
source: We also examined a target region between the linked Myf5 and Myf6 (Mrf4) loci on chromosome 10 that contains several near-perfect octamer sites (not shown), and is strongly bound by Oct4 but not Oct1 (Figure 8E). Oct1 inducibly occupied this region even more rapidly (2 d) as Oct4 binding was lost, and in this case Oct1 binding was maintained, at varying levels, during ESC differentiation (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Oct1 binding to the Myf5/Myf6 region is maintained at varying levels during ESC differentiation.
source: Oct1 inducibly occupied this region even more rapidly (2 d) as Oct4 binding was lost, and in this case Oct1 binding was maintained, at varying levels, during ESC differentiation (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Early Oct1 binding to Pou5f1 is identified and maintained at low levels during the differentiation timecourse.
source: Here early Oct1 binding was identified, which was maintained at low levels during the differentiation timecourse in the case of Pou5f1 but transient in the case of Rest (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Oct1 binding to Rest is transient during differentiation.
source: Here early Oct1 binding was identified, which was maintained at low levels during the differentiation timecourse in the case of Pou5f1 but transient in the case of Rest (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: The results indicate a highly dynamic interplay between Oct1 and Oct4 in differentiating cells.
source: These results indicate a highly dynamic interplay between Oct1 and Oct4 in differentiating cells.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP-qPCR timecourse experiments showing changing Oct1 and Oct4 binding patterns.

claim: Loss of Oct1 results in a failure to fully induce genes associated with a given developmental lineage upon differentiation.
source: Three molecular defects manifest upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient ESCs. First, loss of Oct1 results in a failure to fully induce genes associated with a given developmental lineage.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq and RT-qPCR data showing defective induction of lineage-appropriate genes.

claim: Oct1 is necessary for the repression of alternative embryonic developmental lineages.
source: Second, Oct1 is necessary for the repression of alternative embryonic developmental lineages.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing ectopic expression of lineage-inappropriate genes.

claim: Upon differentiation, Oct1-deficient cells show ectopic expression of genes specific to alternative lineages.
source: As a result, upon differentiation gene expression programs are marked not only by poor induction of lineage-appropriate gene expression, but also by ectopic expression of genes specific to alternative lineages (Figure 8G).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data and model in Figure 8G.

claim: The third molecular defect in Oct1-deficient ESCs is mis-expression of genes associated with extra-embryonic lineages.
source: The third defect is mis-expression of genes associated with extra-embryonic lineages.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data showing expression of placental genes.

claim: Extra-embryonic lineage genes are normally under tight repression in ESCs and their differentiated progeny.
source: These genes are normally under tight repression in ESCs and their differentiated progeny.
evidence: This is established knowledge about extra-embryonic gene regulation.

claim: Prl8a6 and Prl3b1 are mis-expressed in RA-differentiated Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: For example, Prl8a6 and Prl3b1 are mis-expressed in RA-differentiated ESCs.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data in Figure 6F.

claim: The Cdx2 promoter contains a perfect consensus octamer element and is a known Oct1 target in somatic cells.
source: For example, the Cdx2 promoter contains a perfect consensus octamer element and is a known Oct1 target in somatic cells (Jin and Li, 2001; Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin and Li, 2001 and Wang et al., 2009.

claim: In the early embryo, Cdx2 promotes trophectoderm fate and is under tight repression by Oct4.
source: In the early embryo, Cdx2 promotes trophectoderm fate and is under tight repression by Oct4 (Yeap et al., 2009; Yuan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yeap et al., 2009 and Yuan et al., 2009.

claim: Later in development, Cdx2 is induced in the endoderm-derived developing gastrointestinal tract and during primitive hematopoiesis.
source: Later in development, Cdx2 is induced in the endoderm-derived developing gastrointestinal tract (Guo et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2008) and during primitive hematopoiesis (Wang et al., 2008), but is not widely expressed in ectoderm (Suh and Traber, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2008; Suh and Traber, 1996.

claim: Cdx2 is not widely expressed in ectoderm.
source: Later in development, Cdx2 is induced in the endoderm-derived developing gastrointestinal tract (Guo et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2008) and during primitive hematopoiesis (Wang et al., 2008), but is not widely expressed in ectoderm (Suh and Traber, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suh and Traber, 1996.

claim: Cdx2 is mis-expressed following RA-mediated differentiation of both germline and inducible-conditional Oct1-deficient ESCs.
source: Cdx2 is mis-expressed following RA-mediated differentiation of both germline and inducible-conditional Oct1-deficient ESCs.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figures 2B and 4F.

claim: Oct1 may execute the opposite function in extra-embryonic tissue, as germline Oct1-deficient mice show defects in extra-embryonic tissues including poor expression of Cdx2.
source: Interestingly Oct1 may execute the opposite function in extra-embryonic tissue, as germline Oct1-deficient mice show defects in extra-embryonic tissues including poor expression of Cdx2 (Sebastiano et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebastiano et al., 2010.

claim: Oct1 and Oct4 regulate common and distinct targets in ESCs.
source: ChIPseq experiments reveal that Oct1 and Oct4 regulate common and distinct targets in ESCs.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data in Figure 7A.

claim: Differences in bound targets between Oct1 and Oct4 lead to functional consequences, as the two proteins recruit different cofactors.
source: These differences in bound targets lead to functional consequences, as the two proteins recruit different cofactors such as Jmjd1a in the case of Oct1 and Jmjd1c in the case of Oct4 (Shakya et al., 2015a, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shakya et al., 2015a and 2011.

claim: Oct4 occupies a large group of >5000 genes, including developmentally poised genes and core pluripotency genes.
source: Oct4 occupies a large group of >5000 genes, including developmentally poised genes such as Hoxc5 and Myf5, and core pluripotency genes such as Pou5f1 and Nanog.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data in Figure 7A.

claim: Oct1 does not occupy developmentally poised genes or core pluripotency genes in ESCs.
source: Oct1 does not occupy these genes in ESCs, consistent with the ability of Oct1-deficient ESCs to maintain pluripotency.
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data showing lack of Oct1 binding at these genes.

claim: Oct1 co-occupies a cohort of 325 genes with Oct4 that are highly enriched for a motif known as a MORE.
source: Instead Oct1 co-occupies a cohort of 325 genes with Oct4 that are highly enriched for a motif known as a MORE (Reményi et al., 2001; Tomilin et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq and motif analysis in Figure 7A-B, and citations to Reményi et al., 2001 and Tomilin et al., 2000.

claim: Oct proteins are known to homo- and hetero-dimerize.
source: Oct proteins are known to homo- and hetero-dimerize (Kang et al., 2009; Tantin et al., 2008; Tomilin et al., 2000; Verrijzer et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang et al., 2009; Tantin et al., 2008; Tomilin et al., 2000; Verrijzer et al., 1992.

claim: The configuration of Oct proteins can determine cofactor association and hence regulatory output.
source: The configuration of Oct proteins can determine cofactor association and hence regulatory output (Reményi et al., 2001; Tomilin et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reményi et al., 2001 and Tomilin et al., 2000.

claim: Many constitutively co-bound genes were previously shown to become occupied by Oct1 upon oxidative stress exposure in differentiated cells lacking Oct4.
source: Many of these constitutively co-bound genes were previously shown to become occupied by Oct1 upon oxidative stress exposure in differentiated cells lacking Oct4 (Kang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 2009.

claim: Fibroblasts lacking Oct1 show inappropriate repression of MORE-containing genes following H2O2 exposure.
source: Fibroblasts lacking Oct1 show inappropriate repression of MORE-containing genes following H2O2 exposure (Kang et al., 2009; Shakya et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang et al., 2009 and Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Oct1 also exclusively associates with a small number (~200) of other genes including Taf12, which contains another binding site variant known as a TMFORE.
source: Oct1 also exclusively associates with a small number (~200) of other genes including Taf12, which contains another binding site variant known as a TMFORE (Kang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by ChIPseq data and citation to Kang et al., 2009.

claim: Oct4 is present at higher levels in ESCs compared to Oct1.
source: Oct4 is present at higher levels in ESCs compared to Oct1, suggesting that mass action may contribute to the lack of Oct1 binding.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and RNAseq data showing higher Oct4 expression.

claim: Mass action may contribute to the lack of Oct1 binding at developmental targets in ESCs.
source: Oct4 is present at higher levels in ESCs compared to Oct1, suggesting that mass action may contribute to the lack of Oct1 binding.
evidence: This is speculation about why Oct1 doesn't bind these targets in ESCs.

claim: Oct1 transiently replaces Oct4 at many Oct4 target genes upon differentiation.
source: We propose that Oct1 transiently replaces Oct4 at many such Oct4 target genes upon differentiation, where it promotes lineage-appropriate target gene expression, and represses expression of lineage-inappropriate targets.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR timecourse data in Figure 8F.

claim: Oct1 promotes lineage-appropriate target gene expression upon differentiation.
source: We propose that Oct1 transiently replaces Oct4 at many such Oct4 target genes upon differentiation, where it promotes lineage-appropriate target gene expression, and represses expression of lineage-inappropriate targets.
evidence: Inferred from the gene expression defects observed in Oct1-deficient cells.

claim: Oct1 represses expression of lineage-inappropriate targets upon differentiation.
source: We propose that Oct1 transiently replaces Oct4 at many such Oct4 target genes upon differentiation, where it promotes lineage-appropriate target gene expression, and represses expression of lineage-inappropriate targets.
evidence: Inferred from the ectopic expression of lineage-inappropriate genes in Oct1-deficient cells.

claim: Oct1 binding occurs during a brief but important window during which critical decisions about suppression or potentiation of lineage-specific developmental Oct4 target genes are made.
source: The binding events occur during a brief but important window during which critical decisions about suppression or potentiation of lineage-specific developmental Oct4 target genes are made.
evidence: Inferred from the transient nature of Oct1 binding observed in ChIP-qPCR timecourses.

claim: Oct1 binding occurs before many of the affected target genes are induced.
source: Binding also occurs before many of the affected target genes are induced, suggesting that Oct1 is not the principal driver of expression of these genes, but instead establishes a chromatin context in which these genes remain poised for expression, or become permanently repressed.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ChIP-qPCR and gene expression timecourses.

claim: Oct1 is not the principal driver of expression of developmental genes, but instead establishes a chromatin context in which these genes remain poised for expression, or become permanently repressed.
source: Binding also occurs before many of the affected target genes are induced, suggesting that Oct1 is not the principal driver of expression of these genes, but instead establishes a chromatin context in which these genes remain poised for expression, or become permanently repressed.
evidence: This is speculation about Oct1's mechanism of action based on the timing of binding.

claim: Hoxc5 shows poor induction upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient cells.
source: Of the genes tested in ChIP-qPCR RA differentiation timecourses, the lineage-appropriate Hoxc5 gene shows poor induction in upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), Myf5 and Myf6 are mesoderm-specific and lineage-inappropriate, Rest is both pluripotency-associated and lineage-inappropriate, and Pou5f1 is more restricted to ESCs.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Myf5 and Myf6 are mesoderm-specific and lineage-inappropriate for RA differentiation.
source: Of the genes tested in ChIP-qPCR RA differentiation timecourses, the lineage-appropriate Hoxc5 gene shows poor induction in upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), Myf5 and Myf6 are mesoderm-specific and lineage-inappropriate, Rest is both pluripotency-associated and lineage-inappropriate, and Pou5f1 is more restricted to ESCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Myf5 and Myf6 expression patterns.

claim: Rest is both pluripotency-associated and lineage-inappropriate for RA differentiation.
source: Of the genes tested in ChIP-qPCR RA differentiation timecourses, the lineage-appropriate Hoxc5 gene shows poor induction in upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), Myf5 and Myf6 are mesoderm-specific and lineage-inappropriate, Rest is both pluripotency-associated and lineage-inappropriate, and Pou5f1 is more restricted to ESCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rest expression patterns.

claim: Pou5f1 is more restricted to ESCs.
source: Of the genes tested in ChIP-qPCR RA differentiation timecourses, the lineage-appropriate Hoxc5 gene shows poor induction in upon differentiation of Oct1-deficient cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), Myf5 and Myf6 are mesoderm-specific and lineage-inappropriate, Rest is both pluripotency-associated and lineage-inappropriate, and Pou5f1 is more restricted to ESCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Pou5f1 expression patterns.

claim: Lineage-inappropriate genes tested in ChIP-qPCR showed no evidence of ectopic expression in Oct1-deficient cells.
source: These latter genes showed no evidence of ectopic expression.
evidence: Stated in the text based on gene expression analysis.

claim: Redundant mechanisms, perhaps mediated by other Oct proteins such as Oct6/Pou3f1, may enforce repression of some lineage-inappropriate genes in differentiating ESCs.
source: This observation can be reconciled with our model by positing that redundant mechanisms, perhaps mediated by other Oct proteins such as Oct6/Pou3f1, enforce their repression in differentiating ESCs.
evidence: This is speculation about potential redundancy with other Oct proteins.

claim: The bipotential function of Oct1 is consistent with previous findings in fibroblasts and T cells.
source: The bipotential function of Oct1 is consistent with previous findings in fibroblasts and T cells (Shakya et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Oct1 functions are mediated in part through association with the inhibitory chromatin remodeling complex NuRD.
source: Oct1 functions are mediated in part through association with the inhibitory chromatin remodeling complex NuRD (Shakya et al., 2011), or with Jmjd1a/KDM3A, a histone H3K9me2 lysine demethylase (Shakya et al., 2015b, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shakya et al., 2011.

claim: Oct1 functions are mediated in part through association with Jmjd1a/KDM3A, a histone H3K9me2 lysine demethylase.
source: Oct1 functions are mediated in part through association with the inhibitory chromatin remodeling complex NuRD (Shakya et al., 2011), or with Jmjd1a/KDM3A, a histone H3K9me2 lysine demethylase (Shakya et al., 2015b, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shakya et al., 2015b and 2011.

claim: H3K9me2 controls developmental gene induction.
source: H3K9me2 also controls developmental gene induction (Wen et al., 2009; Zylicz et al., 2015) and reprogramming to pluripotency (Chen et al., 2013; Sridharan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wen et al., 2009 and Zylicz et al., 2015.

claim: H3K9me2 controls reprogramming to pluripotency.
source: H3K9me2 also controls developmental gene induction (Wen et al., 2009; Zylicz et al., 2015) and reprogramming to pluripotency (Chen et al., 2013; Sridharan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Sridharan et al., 2013.

claim: The ability of Oct1 to suppress genes for alternative developmental lineages is reminiscent of findings using T cells in which Oct1 suppresses alternative T cell lineage genes via inter-chromosomal communication between gene loci.
source: The ability of Oct1 to suppress genes for alternative developmental lineages is reminiscent of findings using T cells in which Oct1 suppresses alternative T cell lineage genes via inter-chromosomal communication between gene loci that execute opposing gene expression programs (Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: Oct1 interacts with CTCF, helping it foster exclusive gene expression programs in T cells.
source: Oct1 interacts with CTCF (Kim et al., 2014), helping it foster exclusive gene expression programs in T cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2014.

claim: More work is required to determine if Oct1 insures mutually exclusive embryonic developmental gene expression programs through mechanisms similar to those in T cells.
source: More work is required to determine if Oct1 insures mutually exclusive embryonic developmental gene expression programs through similar mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.
